platforms.title: Earplugs Might Be Secretly Behind Your Sound Sensitivity
platforms.meta_description: If chewing or typing sounds feel unbearably loud, wearing earplugs all day might be part of the problem. Blocking sound out can make the brain more sensitive.
platforms.body_html:
If everyday sounds like chewing, typing, or a pen clicking feel unbearably loud and irritating to you while they barely register for everyone else, you may be dealing with misophonia or hyperacusis — and the habit of avoiding sound altogether may be quietly making it worse.

Three Things Tend To Be Behind It

Sound sensitivity like this usually traces back to one or more of three causes: repeated exposure to loud noise, overuse of earplugs or noise avoidance, and migraine or TMJ (jaw joint) problems.

Repeated exposure to loud noise — concerts, construction sites, loud workplaces — can damage the auditory nerve in a way that makes the brain amplify sound signals more than it should. But the less obvious cause is the opposite habit: wearing earplugs all day or constantly seeking out silence. Depriving your ears of normal sound input for long stretches trains the brain to turn up its internal volume, so when sound does get through, it registers as far louder and more grating than it actually is.

Migraine and TMJ disorders add a third path. The trigeminal nerve, which carries pain signals from headaches and jaw joint problems, connects to the same brainstem nuclei that process auditory signals — so when the trigeminal nerve is irritated, the auditory pathway tends to become more reactive too, which is part of why people with migraines so often report sound sensitivity during an attack.

What Actually Reduces Sensitivity — A Quick Checklist

  • Protect your ears only during genuinely loud, triggering situations — concerts, power tools — rather than wearing earplugs as a default.
  • Keep soft background sound on instead of chasing total silence — white noise or ambient sound helps the auditory system stay calibrated to normal input.
  • Get migraine or TMJ symptoms managed if you have them, since calming the trigeminal nerve tends to calm the auditory pathway too.
  • See an ENT specialist if the sensitivity is disrupting daily life, or if it comes with headaches or dizziness that don't improve.

How Common This Really Is

Sound sensitivity like this isn't rare or unusual. A national study out of Duke University found that about 4.6 percent of US adults meet criteria for misophonia, and separate research reviewed in the audiology literature estimates hyperacusis prevalence anywhere from 0.2 to 17 percent of the general population depending on how strictly it's measured. The overlap between the two conditions is substantial too: studies have found misophonia shows up far more often in people who also have hyperacusis than in those who don't, which lines up with how closely the two conditions share triggers and underlying mechanisms. None of this means the problem is imagined or unusual — it's common enough that any ENT practice sees it on a regular basis.

So before reaching for another pair of earplugs to get through the day, it's worth pausing and asking: noise exposure, earplug overuse, migraine or TMJ — which of these three has actually been part of your daily routine, and which one have you never actually addressed?
